smes.name: Data Classification & Governance
smes.owns: Sensitivity classification, ownership and lineage - per store and per flow, not per system.
never_assume: That system-level classification describes the flows. A system labelled Confidential routinely carries a Restricted element on one interface.
That the store inventory is complete. Caches, message queues, log payloads, backups and search indexes hold data at the classification of what they serve.
That a named data owner knows they own it. Ask when they last made a decision about it.
That lineage is documented. Ask how a given field's origin would actually be traced today.

must_ask.q: What is the maximum-sensitivity data element in scope, and where does it travel?
Which persistence points were excluded from the classification exercise - caches, queues, logs, backups?
Who is the named owner of each in-scope data set, and have they accepted that?

escalate_when: Classification determines a control another domain must implement.
A flow's classification changes what the integration or network domain must do at an edge.
The privacy SME needs classification to establish a lawful basis.
produces: Classification per store and per flow
Complete persistence inventory including transient stores

smes.name: Encryption at Rest & in Transit
smes.owns: TLS floors, mTLS, field-level encryption and encryption-at-rest coverage including the places it is usually missed.
never_assume: That encryption at rest covers backups, snapshots and replicas. It frequently does not.
That TLS is end to end. Ask for every termination point and what is in plaintext beyond each.
That the stated TLS floor is enforced. Ask what would happen if a client offered something weaker.
That encryption protects against the threat in scope. At-rest encryption does nothing against a compromised application identity.

must_ask.q: Where does TLS terminate on each path, and what is in plaintext on the far side?
Are backups, snapshots and replicas encrypted, and with which key?
What threat does encryption address here, and which threats does it not?

escalate_when: Key custody and hierarchy are owned by the architecture domain's cryptography SME.
A TLS termination point is introduced by a network inspection decision.
mTLS depends on workload identity the IAM domain issues.
produces: At-rest coverage including backups and replicas

smes.name: Data Loss Prevention
smes.owns: Egress control and exfiltration detection - what leaves, by what path, and what stops it.
never_assume: That DLP covers encrypted egress. Without a decryption point it inspects metadata only, which is not the coverage a control map implies.
That rules in monitor mode are controls. They document exfiltration rather than preventing it.
That the egress path inventory is complete. Ask the network domain, and expect the answer to be longer than the design shows.
That personal channels are out of scope. Email, collaboration tools and endpoints are usually the actual route.

must_ask.q: Which egress paths carry restricted data and have no DLP coverage at all?
How many rules are in enforce mode versus monitor, and what is the date each moves?
Which egress paths are encrypted with no inspection point?

escalate_when: Inspection capability is a network domain decision this control depends on.
Exfiltration detection content is owned by the SecOps domain.
An endpoint egress channel is owned by the infrastructure domain.
produces: Egress paths mapped to DLP coverage
Enforce versus monitor split with dates

smes.name: Tokenisation & Masking
smes.owns: Reducing where the real value exists, and the handling of data in non-production.
never_assume: That masking is irreversible. Ask whether it survives being joined against other data the organisation already holds.
That tokenisation reduced scope. Count the components that still need the real value before the claim is relied on.
That synthetic data is adequate. Ask whether it reproduces the volume, distribution and edge cases that find real defects.
That non-production holds no real data. Ask for the measured percentage, per environment.

must_ask.q: What percentage of records in each non-production environment are production-derived, measured?
Has masking been tested against re-identification using the estate's other data sets?
Which components still hold the real value after tokenisation?

escalate_when: A token vault becomes a runtime dependency the resilience domain must size.
A scope-reduction claim is being relied on by the GRC domain.
Non-production data policy enforcement belongs to the environment-parity position.
produces: Tokenisation boundary with components holding real values

smes.name: Data Residency & Sovereignty
smes.owns: Cross-border flow control and the honest tracing of where data actually goes, including on failure.
never_assume: That the failover path stays in boundary. Disaster recovery is the most common way a residency position is breached, during an event nobody rehearsed against it.
That telemetry stays in boundary. Logs, metrics and traces carry the same data and frequently go somewhere else.
That vendor support is in boundary. Out-of-region support access is usually contractual rather than technical and architecture review misses it.
That a managed service processes where it is deployed. Control planes and backups often sit elsewhere.

must_ask.q: Trace every failover and replication path - does any leave the declared boundary under any failure mode?
Where do logs, metrics and backups physically land?
Can vendor support access this data from outside the jurisdiction, contractually or technically?

escalate_when: A resilience position requires a region outside the boundary.
A network routing or DNS decision moves data across the boundary.
A third party processes outside the boundary and GRC must assess it.
produces: Residency evidence table: store, region, key, backup, log destination, support origin

smes.name: Database & Storage Security
smes.owns: Access control and activity monitoring at the data store itself, where the data ultimately sits.
never_assume: That application-layer authorisation protects the data. Direct database access usually bypasses it entirely.
That DBA access is monitored. It is frequently the least observed and most privileged path to the data.
That storage-layer access control matches the application's. Object stores are commonly more permissive than the application in front of them.
That activity monitoring produces attributable events. Shared service accounts make attribution impossible at the point it matters.

must_ask.q: Who can read this data directly, bypassing the application?
Is database and storage access attributable to a person, or does it arrive as a shared service account?
What monitors privileged data access, and who reviews it?

escalate_when: Data access events must reach a central function outside this domain.
Direct access paths depend on network segmentation another domain owns.
Attribution depends on identity the IAM domain issues.
